claim: Methanogenic archaea use a [NiFe]-hydrogenase, Frh, for oxidation/reduction of F420, an important hydride carrier in the methanogenesis pathway from H2 and CO2.
source: Methanogenic archaea use a [NiFe]-hydrogenase, Frh, for oxidation/reduction of F420, an important hydride carrier in the methanogenesis pathway from H2 and CO2.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about methanogenic archaea and is supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Frh accounts for about 1% of the cytoplasmic protein.
source: Frh accounts for about 1% of the cytoplasmic protein and forms a huge complex consisting of FrhABG heterotrimers with each a [NiFe] center, four Fe-S clusters and an FAD.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the abundance of Frh in the cytoplasm, likely based on prior experimental measurements.

claim: Frh forms a huge complex consisting of FrhABG heterotrimers with each a [NiFe] center, four Fe-S clusters and an FAD.
source: Frh accounts for about 1% of the cytoplasmic protein and forms a huge complex consisting of FrhABG heterotrimers with each a [NiFe] center, four Fe-S clusters and an FAD.
evidence: This describes the composition of the Frh complex based on the structural analysis presented in this study.

claim: The structure of Frh was determined by near-atomic resolution cryo-EM with and without bound substrate F420.
source: Here, we report the structure determined by near-atomic resolution cryo-EM of Frh with and without bound substrate F420.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by the cryo-EM data and analysis presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The polypeptide chains of FrhB, for which there was no homolog, was traced de novo from the EM map.
source: The polypeptide chains of FrhB, for which there was no homolog, was traced de novo from the EM map.
evidence: This describes the methodology used for building the FrhB model, as there was no existing structural template.

claim: The 1.2-MDa complex contains 12 copies of the heterotrimer.
source: The 1.2-MDa complex contains 12 copies of the heterotrimer, which unexpectedly form a spherical protein shell with a hollow core.
evidence: This is a structural finding from the cryo-EM reconstruction showing the oligomeric state of the complex.

claim: The heterotrimers unexpectedly form a spherical protein shell with a hollow core.
source: The 1.2-MDa complex contains 12 copies of the heterotrimer, which unexpectedly form a spherical protein shell with a hollow core.
evidence: This describes the unexpected quaternary structure revealed by the cryo-EM map, contrasting with previous models.

claim: The cryo-EM map reveals strong electron density of the chains of metal clusters running parallel to the protein shell.
source: The cryo-EM map reveals strong electron density of the chains of metal clusters running parallel to the protein shell, and the F420-binding site is located at the end of the chain near the outside of the spherical structure.
evidence: This describes a feature visible in the cryo-EM density map.

claim: The F420-binding site is located at the end of the chain near the outside of the spherical structure.
source: The cryo-EM map reveals strong electron density of the chains of metal clusters running parallel to the protein shell, and the F420-binding site is located at the end of the chain near the outside of the spherical structure.
evidence: This is a structural finding from comparing maps with and without F420 substrate.

claim: [NiFe]-hydrogenases are microbial enzymes that heterolytically cleave H2, after which the electrons from a hydride ion are reversibly transferred to electron carriers.
source: [NiFe]-hydrogenases are microbial enzymes that heterolytically cleave H2, after which the electrons from a hydride ion are reversibly transferred to electron carriers.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of [NiFe]-hydrogenases.

claim: The members of the [NiFe]-hydrogenase family are composed of at least two subunits, large (∼60 kDa) and small (∼30 kDa), which contain a [NiFe] dinuclear metal center and three iron–sulfur (Fe-S) clusters, respectively.
source: The members of the [NiFe]-hydrogenase family are composed of at least two subunits, large (∼60 kDa) and small (∼30 kDa), which contain a [NiFe] dinuclear metal center and three iron–sulfur (Fe-S) clusters, respectively.
evidence: This describes the general composition of [NiFe]-hydrogenases based on established knowledge.

claim: The [NiFe]-hydrogenase family is classified into five distantly related groups based on a phylogenetic analysis of their primary structures.
source: The family is classified into five distantly related groups based on a phylogenetic analysis of their primary structures (Vignais and Billoud, 2007; Constant et al., 2011).
evidence: This classification is supported by cited references.

claim: The cytoplasmic F420-reducing [NiFe]-hydrogenase (Frh) belongs to the group 3 [NiFe]-hydrogenases.
source: The cytoplasmic F420-reducing [NiFe]-hydrogenase (Frh) belongs to the group 3 [NiFe]-hydrogenases, which catalyze the reversible reduction of the soluble hydride carrier, NAD(P) or F420.
evidence: This is a classification statement based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Group 3 [NiFe]-hydrogenases catalyze the reversible reduction of the soluble hydride carrier, NAD(P) or F420.
source: The cytoplasmic F420-reducing [NiFe]-hydrogenase (Frh) belongs to the group 3 [NiFe]-hydrogenases, which catalyze the reversible reduction of the soluble hydride carrier, NAD(P) or F420.
evidence: This describes the catalytic function of group 3 hydrogenases.

claim: F420 is a deazaflavin derivative that acts as an important hydride acceptor/donor in the central methanogenic pathway.
source: F420 is a deazaflavin derivative that acts as an important hydride acceptor/donor in the central methanogenic pathway.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the chemical nature and function of F420.

claim: The group 3 hydrogenases contain an additional subunit that interacts with the soluble coenzymes, for example, the iron–sulfur flavoprotein FrhB.
source: The group 3 hydrogenases contain an additional subunit that interacts with the soluble coenzymes, for example, the iron–sulfur flavoprotein FrhB.
evidence: This describes a distinguishing feature of group 3 hydrogenases compared to other groups.

claim: To date, the crystal structures of [NiFe]-hydrogenases only from group 1 have been determined.
source: To date, the crystal structures of [NiFe]-hydrogenases only from group 1 have been determined: six derived from sulfate-reducing bacteria, including two orthologs harboring a [NiFeSe]-center as active site (Volbeda et al., 1995; Higuchi et al., 1997; Montet et al., 1997; Garcin et al., 1999; Matias et al., 2001; Marques et al., 2010), one from a photosynthetic bacterium (Ogata et al., 2010), and three from hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria and Escherichia coli, which in contrast to the other species are oxygen-tolerant and have an usual [4Fe-3S] proximal cluster (Fritsch et al., 2011; Shomura et al., 2011; Volbeda et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous structural studies.

claim: Frh is a key enzyme in the metabolism of methanogenic archaea.
source: Frh is a key enzyme in the metabolism of methanogenic archaea (Thauer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The reduction of carbon dioxide to methane is an overall eight-electron reduction process involving the oxidation of four molecules of H2 by several hydrogenases.
source: The reduction of carbon dioxide to methane is an overall eight-electron reduction process involving the oxidation of four molecules of H2 by several hydrogenases.
evidence: This describes the stoichiometry of methanogenesis based on established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Four electrons are provided through the reduced form of the coenzyme F420, which is regenerated by Frh.
source: Four electrons are provided through the reduced form of the coenzyme F420, which is regenerated by Frh.
evidence: This describes the role of Frh in the methanogenesis pathway.

claim: Frh is a heterotrimeric enzyme composed of the large subunit FrhA (45 kDa) with a binuclear [NiFe]-center, the small subunit FrhG (26 kDa) with three [4Fe4S] clusters and the iron–sulfur flavoprotein FrhB (31 kDa) with a [4Fe4S] cluster and FAD, and the F420-binding site.
source: Frh is a heterotrimeric enzyme composed of the large subunit FrhA (45 kDa) with a binuclear [NiFe]-center, the small subunit FrhG (26 kDa) with three [4Fe4S] clusters and the iron–sulfur flavoprotein FrhB (31 kDa) with a [4Fe4S] cluster and FAD, and the F420-binding site.
evidence: This describes the subunit composition and cofactor content of Frh based on the structural analysis.

claim: Frh has been shown by electron microscopy to form a huge complex of similar appearance in all species investigated: Methanococcus voltae, Methanospirillum hungatei, Methanobacterium thermoautotrophicum ΔH, and Methanobacterium thermoautotrophicum Marburg.
source: Frh accounts for about 1% of the cytoplasmic protein and has been shown by electron microscopy to form a huge complex of similar appearance in all species investigated: Methanococcus voltae (Muth et al., 1987), Methanospirillum hungatei (Sprott et al., 1987), Methanobacterium thermoautotrophicum ΔH (Wackett et al., 1987), and Methanobacterium thermoautotrophicum Marburg (Braks et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous electron microscopy studies.

claim: From negative stain images, the complex was interpreted as a flat cylinder consisting of an octamer or hexamer of the heterotrimer.
source: From negative stain images, the complex was interpreted as a flat cylinder consisting of an octamer (Wackett et al., 1987) or hexamer (Braks et al., 1994) of the heterotrimer.
evidence: This describes previous interpretations from negative stain EM studies, which are now shown to be incorrect.

claim: Recent developments in instrumentation and image processing software have made it possible to determine structures of large macromolecular complexes to near-atomic resolution by cryo-electron microscopy.
source: Recently, developments in instrumentation and image processing software have made it possible to determine structures of large macromolecular complexes to near-atomic resolution by cryo-electron microscopy.
evidence: This is a general statement about advances in cryo-EM technology.

claim: Most successful have been studies of large icosahedral viruses.
source: Most successful have been studies of large icosahedral viruses (Yu et al., 2008, 2011; Liu et al., 2010; Wolf et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2010a; Chen et al., 2011; Settembre et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to virus structure studies.

claim: A few smaller complexes in the 1 MDa size range of lower symmetry have yielded high-resolution structures, notably GroEL and archaeal chaperonins.
source: but also a few smaller complexes in the 1 MDa size range of lower symmetry have yielded high-resolution structures, notably GroEL (Ludtke et al., 2008) and archaeal chaperonins (Cong et al., 2010, 2012; Zhang et al., 2010b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: The Frh complex is a 1.2-MDa dodecamer with tetrahedral symmetry.
source: The Frh complex is a 1.2-MDa dodecamer with tetrahedral symmetry.
evidence: This is a key structural finding from the cryo-EM analysis.

claim: The location of all cofactors were identified.
source: The location of all cofactors were identified, and the backbone of the three proteins was traced, including FrhB that has a novel fold.
evidence: This describes the completeness of the structural model derived from the cryo-EM map.

claim: The backbone of the three proteins was traced, including FrhB that has a novel fold.
source: The location of all cofactors were identified, and the backbone of the three proteins was traced, including FrhB that has a novel fold.
evidence: This describes the model building process and the discovery that FrhB has a unique structure.

claim: All projections of the Frh complex are ring-shaped with a diameter of ∼16 nm.
source: We found that all projections of the Frh complex are ring-shaped with a diameter of ∼16 nm (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from the electron micrographs shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Class averages showed twofold and threefold symmetry, which is consistent with tetrahedral symmetry.
source: Class averages showed twofold and threefold symmetry (Figure 1B), which is consistent with tetrahedral symmetry.
evidence: This is an inference from the class averages shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The complexes consist of six dimers of FrhABG arranged into a shell around a hollow core, not in a cylindrical arrangement as in previous EM models.
source: We conclude that the complexes consist of six dimers of FrhABG arranged into a shell around a hollow core, not in a cylindrical arrangement as in previous EM models (Wackett et al., 1987; Braks et al., 1994).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the structural analysis that contradicts previous models.

claim: The dodecamer has a total MW of 1.2 MDa.
source: The dodecamer has a total MW of 1.2 MDa.
evidence: This is calculated from the composition of the complex.

claim: Iterative structural refinement of a 84,000-particle cryo-EM dataset, applying tetrahedral symmetry, resulted in a 3D reconstruction at a resolution where the pitch of α-helices and many side chains are recognizable in the map, and β-strands are clearly separated.
source: Iterative structural refinement of a 84,000-particle cryo-EM dataset, applying tetrahedral symmetry, resulted in a 3D reconstruction (Figure 2) at a resolution where the pitch of α-helices and many side chains are recognizable in the map, and β-strands are clearly separated (Figure 2E–G, 5B).
evidence: This describes the quality of the cryo-EM reconstruction based on visible features in the map.

claim: The globular protein complex showed no preferred orientations in the ice, resulting in a homogeneous coverage of angles.
source: The globular protein complex showed no preferred orientations in the ice, resulting in a homogeneous coverage of angles (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown by the Euler angle distribution in Figure 1C.

claim: The map shows six distinct dimers, all clearly separated from one another, sitting on the faces of a cube.
source: The map shows six distinct dimers, all clearly separated from one another (Figure 2C), sitting on the faces of a cube.
evidence: This describes the arrangement visible in the 3D reconstruction shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Each monomer contains a series of five high-density features separated by ∼10 Å, forming an arc in the interior of the protein.
source: Each monomer contains a series of five high-density features separated by ∼10 Å, forming an arc in the interior of the protein (Figure 2D and Video 1).
evidence: This is visible in the cryo-EM map as shown in Figure 2D and Video 1.

claim: These features are easily assigned to the four Fe-S clusters and the [NiFe] center; the latter is recognized by its smaller size.
source: These features are easily assigned to the four Fe-S clusters and the [NiFe] center; the latter is recognized by its smaller size.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the high-density features in the map based on their size and expected composition.

claim: FrhABG contains one approximately 35-Å-long helix on the outer surface and a bundle of four up to 40-Å-long helices at the interface of different dimers, running from the outside to the interior of the complex.
source: FrhABG contains one approximately 35-Å-long helix on the outer surface and a bundle of four up to 40-Å-long helices at the interface of different dimers, running from the outside to the interior of the complex.
evidence: This describes structural features visible in the cryo-EM map.

claim: The large subunit FrhA has considerable homology to the known large subunit structures.
source: The large subunit FrhA has considerable homology to the known large subunit structures (Figure 3)
evidence: This is shown by sequence alignment and structural comparison in Figure 3.

claim: FrhA is characterized by four long α-helices.
source: The large subunit FrhA has considerable homology to the known large subunit structures (Figure 3), and is characterized by four long α-helices.
evidence: This is a structural feature visible in the model.

claim: Docking the large subunit of the group 1 enzyme into the map provides a good fit for the α-helix bundle, with the [NiFe] center correctly situated in its identified location and many other structural elements of FrhA matching closely, including two three-stranded antiparallel β-sheets.
source: Docking the large subunit of the group 1 enzyme into the map provides a good fit for the α-helix bundle, with the [NiFe] center correctly situated in its identified location and many other structural elements of FrhA matching closely, including two three-stranded antiparallel β-sheets.
evidence: This describes the modeling approach and the quality of fit between the homologous structure and the cryo-EM map.

claim: FrhA is about 15 kDa smaller than the large subunits of known structure; all missing elements are located on the periphery.
source: FrhA is about 15 kDa smaller than the large subunits of known structure; all missing elements are located on the periphery.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the FrhA sequence and structure with group 1 hydrogenases.

claim: All but the first three amino acids in the sequence could be traced in the maps.
source: All but the first three amino acids in the sequence could be traced in our maps.
evidence: This describes the completeness of the FrhA model.

claim: The [NiFe] center is located near four cysteine residues, Cys 63, 66, 380, and 383, which are fully conserved in all [NiFe]-hydrogenases.
source: The [NiFe] center is located near four cysteine residues, Cys 63, 66, 380, and 383, which are fully conserved in all [NiFe]-hydrogenases.
evidence: This describes the coordination of the [NiFe] center based on the model and sequence conservation.

claim: The group 1 [NiFe]-hydrogenases contain another ion, typically either Mg2+ or Fe2+/3+.
source: The group 1 [NiFe]-hydrogenases contain another ion, typically either Mg2+ or Fe2+/3+ (Higuchi et al., 1997; Garcin et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: In the Frh map, there is strong density at the position of the additional ion, which is part of the structurally conserved region of FrhA.
source: In our map, there is strong density at this position (Figure 5D), which is part of the structurally conserved region of FrhA, and its surrounding residues, Glu44, Glu229, and His386, are fully conserved in FrhA (Figure 3A), so we interpret this density as an ion.
evidence: This is based on density visible in the cryo-EM map and sequence conservation.

claim: One of the helices of the four-helix bundle has a pronounced kink.
source: One of the helices of the four-helix bundle has a pronounced kink.
evidence: This is a structural feature visible in the model.

claim: This helix was interpreted as residues 166–193, and a proline residue (Pro180) not present in the group I proteins was found exactly at the position of the kink, supporting the assignment.
source: This helix was interpreted as residues 166–193, and a proline residue (Pro180) not present in the group I proteins was found exactly at the position of the kink, supporting the assignment.
evidence: The presence of proline at the kink position supports the sequence assignment.

claim: No density is present beyond His386, and there is no room in the structure for the final 19 amino acids of the protein.
source: No density is present beyond His386, and there is no room in the structure for the final 19 amino acids of the protein.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM map.

claim: The C-terminal residues after the equivalent histidine in [NiFe]-hydrogenases are enzymatically removed during maturation of the enzymes.
source: The C-terminal residues after the equivalent histidine in [NiFe]-hydrogenases are enzymatically removed during maturation of the enzymes (Menon et al., 1993; Theodoratou et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on hydrogenase maturation.

claim: FrhA is posttranslationally modified in the same way, likely by FrhD, a homologous endopeptidase contained in the Frh operon FrhADGB.
source: We can conclude that FrhA is posttranslationally modified in the same way, likely by FrhD, a homologous endopeptidase contained in the Frh operon FrhADGB (Liesegang et al., 2010; Thauer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on the missing C-terminal density and the presence of a homologous protease in the operon.

claim: The fit of the small subunit of the group 1 enzyme reveals structural homology to the N-terminal domain of FrhG including the proximal Fe-S cluster.
source: The fit of the small subunit of the group 1 enzyme reveals structural homology to the N-terminal domain of FrhG including the proximal Fe-S cluster.
evidence: This describes the modeling approach for FrhG using a homologous structure.

claim: Some peripheral helices present in the group 1 protein are missing in the FrhG structure, and the similarity is generally lower than for the large subunit.
source: Some peripheral helices present in the group 1 protein are missing in the FrhG structure, and the similarity is generally lower than for the large subunit (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The N-terminal domain is characterized by a conserved parallel β-sheet flanked by short α-helices.
source: The N-terminal domain is characterized by a conserved parallel β-sheet flanked by short α-helices (Figure 4B).
evidence: This describes a structural feature visible in the model shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In the group 1 [NiFe]-hydrogenases, the proximal Fe-S cluster is located at the C-terminal end of the β-sheet and is coordinated by four cysteines.
source: In the group 1 [NiFe]-hydrogenases, the proximal Fe-S cluster is located at the C-terminal end of the β-sheet and is coordinated by four cysteines.
evidence: This is established knowledge about group 1 hydrogenases.

claim: In the primary structure of FrhG, one of the conserved cysteine residues for the coordination of this cluster is replaced by Asp60.
source: In the primary structure of FrhG, one of the conserved cysteine residues for the coordination of this cluster is replaced by Asp60 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Aspartates have been identified before as ligands of [4Fe4S] clusters.
source: The bacterial hydrogenases as well as most of the archaeal species have a cysteine at this position, but aspartates have been identified before as ligands of [4Fe4S] clusters (Calzolai et al., 1995; Muraki et al., 2010; Gruner et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The C-terminal domain of FrhG has no homology to the group 1 [NiFe]-hydrogenases.
source: The C-terminal domain of FrhG has no homology to the group 1 [NiFe]-hydrogenases.
evidence: This is based on sequence and structural comparison.

claim: The sequence indicates a ferredoxin domain, with two CxxCxxCxxxC sequences coordinating two [4Fe4S] clusters.
source: Instead, the sequence indicates a ferredoxin domain, with two CxxCxxCxxxC sequences coordinating two [4Fe4S] clusters (Figure 6A) (Alex et al., 1990).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and a citation to previous work.

claim: In the model, the residues 235–244 form a β-hairpin with Gly240 at the turn.
source: In our model, the residues 235–244 form a β-hairpin with Gly240 at the turn.
evidence: This describes a structural feature in the model.

claim: The two β-strands were predicted and the hairpin is clearly visible in the density, confirming the assignment.
source: The two β-strands were predicted and the hairpin is clearly visible in the density, confirming the assignment.
evidence: The agreement between prediction and observed density supports the model.

claim: Density of FrhG for a 12-residue stretch (188–199) is missing.
source: Unlike FrhA, which could be traced over its full length, density of FrhG for a 12-residue stretch (188–199) is missing (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM map.

claim: This region is located at the surface and may be disordered.
source: This region is located at the surface and may be disordered.
evidence: This is speculation based on the missing density and surface location.

claim: FrhG as deduced from the M. marburgensis genome sequence is 275 residues long, but no density is present for the 45 N-terminal amino acids.
source: FrhG as deduced from the M. marburgensis genome sequence is 275 residues long (Liesegang et al., 2010), but no density is present for the 45 N-terminal amino acids.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the genome sequence with the observed density.

claim: The frhG gene most probably starts with the initiation codon GTG annotated as Val39 in the genome sequence, which means that density is missing in the map for only the first seven amino acids of FrhG.
source: The frhG gene most probably starts with the initiation codon GTG annotated as Val39 in the genome sequence (Fox et al., 1987; Alex et al., 1990), which means that density is missing in the map for only the first seven amino acids of FrhG.
evidence: This is an inference based on alternative start codon usage supported by citations.

claim: FrhB contains one Fe-S cluster, an FAD, and the F420-binding site.
source: FrhB contains one Fe-S cluster, an FAD, and the F420-binding site.
evidence: This describes the cofactor content of FrhB based on the structural analysis.

claim: There is no homolog of known structure for FrhB.
source: There is no homolog of known structure.
evidence: This is based on structural database searches.

claim: FrhB was traced ab initio, aided by secondary structure predictions and recognizable features in the map that included 10 α-helices, 11 β-strands, and the Fe-S cluster.
source: FrhB was therefore traced ab initio, aided by secondary structure predictions (Figure 7) and recognizable features in the map that included 10 α-helices, 11 β-strands, and the Fe-S cluster.
evidence: This describes the de novo model building approach for FrhB.

claim: The most prominent feature of FrhB is a ∼35 Å surface helix that corresponds to the predicted 24-residue C-terminal helix.
source: The most prominent feature of FrhB is a ∼35 Å surface helix that corresponds to the predicted 24-residue C-terminal helix.
evidence: This describes a structural feature visible in the map that matches the prediction.

claim: No structural homology was found between FrhB and F420-binding proteins of known structure in the protein databank.
source: We examined the F420-binding proteins of known structure in the protein databank, and found no structural homology with FrhB.
evidence: This is based on structural database searches.

claim: All F420-binding proteins of known structure have cofactors different from FAD, for example, methylene-H4MPT or NADP.
source: All these proteins have cofactors different from FAD, for example, methylene-H4MPT or NADP (Ceh et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: No homologous FAD-binding proteins were found.
source: Also no homologous FAD-binding proteins were found.
evidence: This is based on structural database searches.

claim: FrhB has a novel fold.
source: We conclude that FrhB has a novel fold (Figure 4C and Video 4).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the lack of structural homologs.

claim: The Fe-S cluster is most probably a 4Fe-4S cluster because it is surrounded by four cysteines (Cys 104, 134, 192, and 195), which are all fully conserved.
source: The Fe-S cluster is most probably a 4Fe-4S cluster because it is surrounded by four cysteines (Cys 104, 134, 192, and 195), which are all fully conserved (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on the coordination geometry and sequence conservation.

claim: The core of FrhB is a mixed six-stranded β-sheet.
source: The core of FrhB is a mixed six-stranded β-sheet.
evidence: This describes a structural feature of the FrhB model.

claim: A density located ∼8 Å from the Fe-S cluster could be interpreted as the isoalloxazine ring of the FAD cofactor.
source: A density located ∼8 Å from the Fe-S cluster could be interpreted as the isoalloxazine ring of the FAD cofactor.
evidence: This is an interpretation of density in the cryo-EM map.

claim: The pyrophosphate moiety is located at the N-terminal end of an α-helix, which is a common FAD-binding motif where the dipole of the helix compensates the negative charge.
source: The pyrophosphate moiety is located at the N-terminal end of an α-helix, which is a common FAD-binding motif where the dipole of the helix compensates the negative charge (Dym and Eisenberg, 2001) (Figure 8)
evidence: This is based on a known structural motif supported by a citation.

claim: The FAD has a bent conformation, with the adenine and isoalloxazine ring only 4–5 Å apart near the highly conserved loop Lys75-Tyr76.
source: The FAD has a bent conformation, with the adenine and isoalloxazine ring only 4–5 Å apart (Figure 8) near the highly conserved loop Lys75-Tyr76.
evidence: This describes the conformation of FAD in the model shown in Figure 8.

claim: The FAD is completely surrounded by highly conserved protein regions, further verifying the backbone trace.
source: The FAD is completely surrounded by highly conserved protein regions (Figure 7 and Video 5), further verifying the backbone trace.
evidence: Sequence conservation around the FAD supports the correctness of the model.

claim: Of the three proteins, only FrhG is missing density for an internal stretch, residues 188–199.
source: Of the three proteins, only FrhG is missing density for an internal stretch, residues 188–199 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM map.

claim: The flanking residues of this stretch are located less than 10 Å apart on the surface of the complex and they probably form a flexible loop.
source: The flanking residues of this stretch are located less than 10 Å apart on the surface of the complex and they probably form a flexible loop.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proximity of flanking residues and surface location.

claim: FrhA and FrhB were traced over their full length.
source: FrhA and FrhB were traced over their full length.
evidence: This describes the completeness of the models for these subunits.

claim: All three proteins follow the rule that hydrophobic residues form the core of the protein and charged residues face the outside.
source: All three proteins follow the rule that hydrophobic residues form the core of the protein and charged residues face the outside.
evidence: This is a general principle of protein structure that is observed in the models.

claim: Several pockets lined with hydrophobic side chains were found, not just in FrhA and FrhG, where these features are shared with the bacterial protein used as a template for modeling, but also in FrhB.
source: We found several pockets lined with hydrophobic side chains, not just in FrhA and FrhG, where these features are shared with the bacterial protein used as a template for modeling, but also in FrhB.
evidence: This describes structural features that support the correctness of the models.

claim: FrhB contains a highly hydrophobic helix (27GIVTGLLAYAL), which is buried completely inside the subunit.
source: FrhB also contains a highly hydrophobic helix (27GIVTGLLAYAL), which is buried completely inside the subunit.
evidence: This describes a structural feature consistent with proper protein folding.

claim: These features all indicate a correct chain trace.
source: These features all indicate a correct chain trace.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple structural features.

claim: Each heterotrimer encompasses a complete electron transfer chain that runs from the [NiFe] cluster in FrhA via the three Fe-S clusters in FrhG and one Fe-S cluster and FAD in FrhB to F420.
source: Our structure shows that each heterotrimer encompasses a complete electron transfer chain that runs from the [NiFe] cluster in FrhA via the three Fe-S clusters in FrhG and one Fe-S cluster and FAD in FrhB to F420 (Figures 4D, 11 and Video 6).
evidence: This describes the arrangement of cofactors for electron transfer based on the structure.

claim: The cofactors describe a curvilinear path in the protein interior, almost parallel to the surface of the complex, with distances of ∼10 Å between neighbors, except FAD and F420, which are in van der Waals contact to enable hydride transfer.
source: The cofactors describe a curvilinear path in the protein interior, almost parallel to the surface of the complex, with distances of ∼10 Å between neighbors, except FAD and F420, which are in van der Waals contact to enable hydride transfer (Figure 8C).
evidence: This describes the spatial arrangement of cofactors shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The predicted F420-binding site is located on the outside of the complex, which facilitates access of the cytosolic F420.
source: The predicted F420-binding site is located on the outside of the complex, which facilitates access of the cytosolic F420.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional significance of the F420 binding site location.

claim: The two electron transfer chains in a dimer are separated by at least 17 Å and are thus independent of each other.
source: The two electron transfer chains in a dimer are separated by at least 17 Å and are thus independent of each other, indicating that the functional unit is one FrhABG heterotrimer and there is no cooperativity in the complex.
evidence: This is based on distance measurements in the structure.

claim: The functional unit is one FrhABG heterotrimer and there is no cooperativity in the complex.
source: The two electron transfer chains in a dimer are separated by at least 17 Å and are thus independent of each other, indicating that the functional unit is one FrhABG heterotrimer and there is no cooperativity in the complex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the separation of electron transfer chains.

claim: The three proteins in the Frh heterotrimer form a tight complex with extensive subunit interfaces and a large number of subunit interactions, including two salt bridges between loops of the two FrhA molecules in a dimer, from Asp312 of one FrhA and Arg314 of the other.
source: The three proteins in the Frh heterotrimer form a tight complex with extensive subunit interfaces and a large number of subunit interactions, including two salt bridges between loops of the two FrhA molecules in a dimer, from Asp312 of one FrhA and Arg314 of the other (Figure 5C).
evidence: This describes interactions visible in the structure shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The heterotrimer is quite slender compared to the two-subunit [NiFe] hydrogenases of known structure, with a small contact surface especially between FrhB and the other two subunits.
source: The heterotrimer is quite slender compared to the two-subunit [NiFe] hydrogenases of known structure, with a small contact surface especially between FrhB and the other two subunits (Figure 12)
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 12.

claim: Complex formation may be necessary for stability of the complex and keeping the metal clusters at optimal distances.
source: and complex formation may be necessary for stability of the complex and keeping the metal clusters at optimal distances.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of complex formation.

claim: The same quaternary structure of Frh has been observed not only in the closely related thermophile M. thermautotrophicus but also in the phylogenetically distant mesophilic M. voltae and M. hungatei.
source: The same quaternary structure of Frh has been observed not only in the closely related thermophile M. thermautotrophicus (Wackett et al., 1987) but also in the phylogenetically distant mesophilic M. voltae (Muth et al., 1987) and M. hungatei (Sprott et al., 1987)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous EM studies.

claim: The formation of a large complex plays an essential role for the function of Frh.
source: so it is clear that the formation of a large complex plays an essential role for the function of Frh.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conservation of the quaternary structure across species.

claim: Icosahedral viruses were reconstructed in recent years to better than 4 Å resolution.
source: icosahedral viruses were reconstructed in recent years to better than 4 Å resolution (Yu et al., 2008, 2011, Zhang et al., 2008, 2010a; Liu et al., 2010; Wolf et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2011; Settembre et al., 2011; )
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to virus structure studies.

claim: The 60-fold symmetry and huge size (∼20 to 150 MDa) of icosahedral viruses contribute to the relatively high signal-to-noise ratio for these particles that makes the determination of the orientation unambiguous.
source: taking advantage of the 60-fold symmetry and huge size (∼20 to 150 MDa), which together contribute to the relatively high signal-to-noise ratio for these particles that makes the determination of the orientation unambiguous.
evidence: This explains why icosahedral viruses are particularly amenable to high-resolution cryo-EM.

claim: For GroEL, subnanometer resolution was reached for the first time in 2004 and ∼4 Å in 2008.
source: For smaller complexes, the techniques have been pioneered with the 800-kDa GroEL complex with D7 symmetry, reaching subnanometer resolution for the first time in 2004 (Ludtke et al., 2004) and ∼4 Å in 2008 (Ludtke et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the GroEL structure studies.

claim: Subsequent reconstructions to ∼4 Å resolution were achieved for archaeal and mammalian chaperonins.
source: Subsequent reconstructions to this resolution were achieved for archaeal (Zhang et al., 2010b) and mammalian (Cong et al., 2010) chaperonins.
evidence: This is supported by citations to chaperonin structure studies.

claim: The chaperonins have different conformational states, and usually only one of these gave a high-resolution map, whereas for the others the resolution was limited due to conformational flexibility.
source: The chaperonins have different conformational states, and usually only one of these gave a high-resolution map, whereas for the others the resolution was limited due to conformational flexibility.
evidence: This is based on knowledge from previous chaperonin structure studies.

claim: The appearance of the Frh reconstructions is similar to the chaperonins.
source: The appearance of our reconstructions is similar to the chaperonins
evidence: This is a qualitative comparison of the cryo-EM maps.

claim: Fourier shell correlation indicates a resolution of 3.9 and 4.0 Å for the two maps, respectively.
source: in agreement with this, Fourier shell correlation indicates a resolution of 3.9 and 4.0 Å for the two maps, respectively (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is based on FSC analysis shown in Figure 10A.

claim: The resolution of such reconstructions are usually overestimated due to correlation of noise at high resolution.
source: Recently it has been noted that the resolution of such reconstructions are usually overestimated due to correlation of noise at high resolution (Scheres and Chen, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a methodological paper.

claim: Using a 'gold standard' procedure to estimate resolution yielded 5.5 Å.
source: Using a 'gold standard' procedure to estimate resolution, where two half-data sets are independently refined to a reference not containing high-resolution information (see 'Materials and methods'), yielded 5.5 Å (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is based on an alternative resolution estimation method shown in Figure 10B.

claim: The α-helical pitch of 5.4 Å is very well defined in many regions.
source: However, an objective indication of (local) resolution is provided by the appearance of secondary structure: the α-helical pitch of 5.4 Å is very well defined in many regions (Figure 2F,G)
evidence: This is visible in the cryo-EM map shown in Figure 2F,G.

claim: The separation of β-strands (axial distance ∼4.8 Å) is clearly visible.
source: as is the separation of β-strands (axial distance ∼4.8 Å) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is visible in the cryo-EM map shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Comparison of well-resolved areas with maps calculated from the model low-pass filtered to different resolutions suggest a resolution ∼4.5 Å.
source: Comparison of these areas with maps calculated from the model low-pass filtered to different resolutions suggest a resolution ∼4.5 Å.
evidence: This is based on comparison with simulated maps.

claim: The overall resolution estimate is an average of well-resolved protein regions and other regions that are less well resolved, especially those at the periphery of the complex.
source: The overall resolution estimate is an average of these well-resolved protein regions and other regions that are less well resolved, especially those at the periphery of the complex.
evidence: This explains the variation in local resolution across the map.

claim: An FSC curve between the experimental map and a map calculated from the model indicated a resolution of 5.8 Å.
source: An FSC curve between the experimental map and a map calculated from the model indicated a resolution of 5.8 Å (Figure 10C)
evidence: This is based on FSC analysis shown in Figure 10C.

claim: This figure constitutes an average over the whole structure, with the model probably best for internal α-helices and worst for loops at the periphery.
source: this figure also constitutes an average over the whole structure, with the model probably best for internal α-helices and worst for loops at the periphery.
evidence: This is an inference about the quality of different regions of the model.

claim: The model-to-map correlation does not properly reflect the resolution of the map, but rather describes how well the model explains the map densities, since the model was derived from the map.
source: Since the model was derived from the map, and not from an independent experiment, this measure does not properly reflect the resolution of the map, but rather describes how well our admittedly incomplete model explains the map densities.
evidence: This is a methodological consideration about the interpretation of model-to-map FSC.

claim: Tight protein structure restraints were used during modeling to prevent overfitting to noise while creating an unrealistic model.
source: It should be noted that we used tight protein structure restraints during modeling, in order to prevent overfitting to noise while creating an unrealistic model that would have yielded a higher model-to-map correlation.
evidence: This describes the modeling strategy used.

claim: Several factors contributed to the successful structure determination of Frh.
source: Several factors contributed to the successful structure determination of Frh.
evidence: This introduces a discussion of factors contributing to success.

claim: The tetrahedral symmetry means that there are 12 asymmetric units in each particle.
source: The tetrahedral symmetry means that there are 12 asymmetric units in each particle, less than the 14 and 16 in the D7 and D8 symmetric chaperonins
evidence: This is a mathematical consequence of tetrahedral symmetry.

claim: The ball-like shape ensures that the complex has no preferential orientation in the ice, unlike the cylinder-shaped chaperonins that tend to be oriented with their symmetry axis parallel or perpendicular to the ice.
source: but the resulting ball-like shape ensures that the complex has no preferential orientation in the ice (Figure 1D), unlike the cylinder-shaped chaperonins that tend to be oriented with their symmetry axis parallel or perpendicular to the ice (Ludtke et al., 2001; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the Euler angle distribution in Figure 1D and citations about chaperonin orientation.

claim: The complex is very rigid.
source: From the quality of the reconstructions, we conclude that the complex is very rigid.
evidence: This is inferred from the high quality of the reconstructions.

claim: The maps of Frh with and without substrate are of similar resolution and quality, implying that any protein conformational changes due to F420 binding are too small to detect at the present resolution.
source: The maps of Frh with and without substrate are of similar resolution and quality, implying that any protein conformational changes due to F420 binding are too small to detect at the present resolution.
evidence: This is an inference from the similarity of the two maps.

claim: The density for F420 is weak, but its position was inferred at an early stage of the analysis from the fact that maps of Frh without the substrate were consistently empty and maps with F420 always showed some density here.
source: The density for F420 is weak, but its position was inferred at an early stage of the analysis from the fact that maps of Frh without the substrate were consistently empty and maps with F420 always showed some density here.
evidence: This describes how the F420 binding site was identified by difference mapping.

claim: The later tracing of the amino acid chain of FrhB and the FAD confirmed the assignment: F420 is in van der Waals distance from its hydride donor, the FAD isoalloxazine ring, and the residues in the vicinity are highly conserved in FrhB and in the FrhB family of F420-binding proteins.
source: The later tracing of the amino acid chain of FrhB and the FAD confirmed the assignment: F420 is in van der Waals distance from its hydride donor, the FAD isoalloxazine ring, and the residues in the vicinity are highly conserved in FrhB and in the FrhB family of F420-binding proteins (Figures 7, 9 and Video 5).
evidence: The model building and sequence conservation support the F420 binding site assignment.

claim: The visibility of the FeS cluster density made it possible to use the four Fe-S ligand cysteines together with a secondary structure prediction as an initial guide for building FrhB.
source: The visibility of the FeS cluster density (Figure 2D and Video 1) made it possible to use the four Fe-S ligand cysteines together with a secondary structure prediction as an initial guide
evidence: This describes the strategy for de novo model building of FrhB.

claim: Large side chain densities helped to establish the correct sequence assignment.
source: large side chain densities helped to establish the correct sequence assignment.
evidence: Visible side chains in the map support the sequence assignment.

claim: The secondary structure prediction was fully confirmed.
source: The secondary structure prediction was fully confirmed
evidence: The observed secondary structure matches the prediction.

claim: Weak or discontinuous densities in the map were almost invariably found to represent glycine residues, further indicating a correct assignment.
source: and weak or discontinuous densities in the map were almost invariably found to represent glycine residues, further indicating a correct assignment.
evidence: The correlation between weak density and glycine positions supports the model.

claim: Density for the FAD cofactor only became clear when most of the protein chain was placed.
source: Density for the FAD cofactor only became clear when most of the protein chain was placed
evidence: This describes the progression of model building.

claim: Density for the ribose and ribitol of FAD are missing.
source: density for the ribose and ribitol are missing (Figure 8).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM map shown in Figure 8.

claim: The N-terminus of helix 26–64 of FrhB is one of the most conserved regions in the FrhB family.
source: The N-terminus of this helix is one of the most conserved regions in the FrhB family (Figures 7, 9)
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment shown in Figures 7 and 9.

claim: The role of the N-terminal helix in compensating the negative charge of the phosphates is a common motif in FAD-binding proteins.
source: and its role in compensating the negative charge of the phosphates is a common motif in FAD-binding proteins (Dym and Eisenberg, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review on FAD-binding motifs.

claim: Conserved regions of FrhB were found near the FAD and surrounding the F420-binding site and its putative entrance channel.
source: Conserved regions of FrhB were found near the FAD and surrounding the F420-binding site and its putative entrance channel (Video 5).
evidence: This is shown in Video 5 with conserved residues highlighted.

claim: All three proteins follow the rule that hydrophobic residues form the core of the protein and charged residues face the outside.
source: All three proteins follow the rule that hydrophobic residues form the core of the protein and charged residues face the outside.
evidence: This is a general principle of protein structure observed in the models.

claim: The residues coordinating the Fe-S cluster, FAD, and F420 are conserved in the FrhB family, which includes subunits of F420-dependent sulfite reductase (Fsr), F420H2:quinone oxidoreductase (FqoF), F420H2:phenazine oxidoreductase (FpoF), F420-dependent glutamate synthase and formate dehydrogenase (FdhB).
source: The residues coordinating the Fe-S cluster, FAD, and F420 are conserved in the FrhB family, which includes subunits of F420-dependent sulfite reductase (Fsr), F420H2:quinone oxidoreductase (FqoF), F420H2:phenazine oxidoreductase (FpoF), F420-dependent glutamate synthase and formate dehydrogenase (FdhB) (Johnson and Mukhopadhyay, 2005) (Figure 9).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 9 and a citation.

claim: Some of these proteins contain additional domains, like an N-terminal ferredoxin domain (which in Frh is part of FrhG), or a C-terminal domain containing a binding site for the substrate of the electron transfer from F420.
source: Some of these proteins contain additional domains, like an N-terminal ferredoxin domain (which in Frh is part of FrhG), or a C-terminal domain containing a binding site for the substrate of the electron transfer from F420.
evidence: This describes variations in domain architecture within the FrhB family.

claim: These enzymes share a common fold with FrhB.
source: Clearly, these enzymes share a common fold with FrhB.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequence conservation of key functional residues.

claim: Methanothermobacter marburgensis was grown anaerobically at 65°C on 80% H2/20% CO2/0.1% H2S in a 12-L fermenter containing 10 L complete mineral salt medium.
source: The archaeon was grown anaerobically at 65°C on 80% H2/20% CO2/0.1% H2S in a 12-L fermenter containing 10 L complete mineral salt medium (Schönheit et al., 1980).
evidence: This describes the cultivation conditions used in the study.

claim: Purification was performed under strictly anaerobic conditions at 18°C in an anaerobic chamber.
source: Purification was performed under strictly anaerobic conditions at 18°C in an anaerobic camper (Coy Laboratory Products, Grass Lake, MI).
evidence: This describes the purification conditions.

claim: All buffers used contained 2 mM DTT and 25 µM FAD.
source: All buffers used contained 2 mM DTT and 25 µM FAD.
evidence: This describes the buffer composition used during purification.

claim: The final data set of substrate-free Frh contained 84,000 particles from 101 negatives of the 402 scanned negatives.
source: The final data set of substrate-free Frh contained 84,000 particles from 101 negatives of the 402 scanned negatives.
evidence: This describes the size of the dataset used for reconstruction.

claim: Ninety seven thousand particles were selected from 80 negatives for the F420 dataset.
source: Ninety seven thousand particles were selected from 80 negatives.
evidence: This describes the size of the F420-bound dataset.

claim: B-factors of the reconstructions were estimated as 54 Å2 for the substrate-free map and 60 Å2 for the map with F420.
source: B-factors of the reconstructions were estimated with the program embfactor (Rosenthal and Henderson, 2003; Fernández et al., 2008) in the resolution range 10–4.5 Å as 54 Å2 for the substrate-free map and 60 Å2 for the map with F420 (see Figure 10D).
evidence: This is based on analysis shown in Figure 10D.

claim: The final model contains 878 residues out of a possible 903.
source: The final model contains 878 residues out of a possible 903, a [NiFe] cluster, 4 [4Fe4S] clusters, an FAD and part of an F420 molecule
evidence: This describes the completeness of the final model.

claim: 88.1% of residues lie in the most favored regions of a Ramachandran plot, 8.0% in generously allowed regions, and 3.8% are outliers.
source: 88.1% of residues lie in the most favored regions of a Ramachandran plot, 8.0% in generously allowed regions, and 3.8% are outliers.
evidence: This describes the stereochemical quality of the model.
